name: Ahaz
bio:
Ahaz succeeded his father Jotham as king of Judah after Jotham was buried in the City of David (2 Kings 15:38).

## 📖 Core Story: Syro-Ephraimite Siege, and Tribute to Assyria

Ahaz reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem but did not do right like his ancestor David; he walked in the ways of Israel's kings, even making his own son pass through fire in pagan sacrifice, and offered sacrifices at the high places and under every green tree. Rezin, king of Syria, and Pekah, king of Israel, besieged Jerusalem but couldn't overcome Ahaz, though Rezin recovered Elath for Syria and drove out the Jews there (2 Kings 16:5-6).

Chronicles describes the scale of this crisis in far greater detail. Pekah's army killed 120,000 of Judah's valiant men in a single day and carried off 200,000 women and children as captives, along with great plunder, including the king's own son Maaseiah, the palace governor Azrikam, and the king's second-in-command Elkanah, all slain by an Ephraimite warrior named Zichri. But the prophet Oded met Israel's returning army at Samaria and rebuked them for their rage, warning that enslaving their own kinsmen would only add to Israel's own guilt before the LORD; moved by this and by four Ephraimite leaders who backed him, the army released the captives, clothed and fed them from the plunder, and carried the weak back to Jericho on donkeys. Edom and the Philistines also raided Judah in this same crisis, worsening Ahaz's humiliation (2 Chronicles 28:5-19). Ahaz sent to Tiglath-Pileser, king of Assyria, calling himself his servant and son, and sent him silver and gold from the temple and palace as tribute, begging rescue from Syria and Israel. Assyria obliged, attacking Damascus, deporting its people, and killing Rezin (2 Kings 16:1-9).

After visiting Damascus to meet Tiglath-Pileser, Ahaz saw a pagan altar there and sent its design back to Urijah the priest, who built a matching altar in the temple before Ahaz returned. Ahaz began using this new altar for all the regular sacrifices, demoting the LORD's own bronze altar, and stripped various bronze temple fixtures, sending some of them away to please the king of Assyria (2 Kings 16:10-18). Chronicles adds that Assyria's help brought Ahaz only distress, not relief, and that in his desperation he sacrificed to the very gods of Damascus that had defeated him, reasoning that since they had helped Syria's kings, they might help him too — a decision Chronicles says ruined him. He also stripped and smashed the temple's furnishings, shut its doors entirely, and built pagan altars on every street corner of Jerusalem and high places in every town of Judah (2 Chronicles 28:20-25). Ahaz died and was buried in the city of Jerusalem, but not among the kings of Israel, and his son Hezekiah succeeded him (2 Kings 16:19-20).
